name: Brazil (Republic)
summary: The largest country in South America, a republic since the monarchy was overthrown in 1889. It has had long periods of democracy and of military rule (1964–1985).

knownFor.label: Brasília
knownFor.note: A planned capital built in about four years, designed by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer.

knownFor.label: Samba and Carnival
knownFor.note: Music and street festivals with African, Portuguese and Indigenous roots.

knownFor.label: Coffee
knownFor.note: Brazil has been the world’s largest coffee producer since the 19th century.

location.value: Eastern South America; about 8.5 million km², almost half of the continent.

terrain.value: The Amazon basin in the north, the Brazilian Highlands, the Pantanal wetlands and a long Atlantic coast.

climate.value: Mostly tropical; hot and wet in the Amazon, drier in the north-east (the sertão), milder in the south.

resources.value: Farmland, rainforest, iron ore, oil (offshore since the 2000s), hydroelectric power and huge rivers.

disasters.value: Droughts in the north-east, floods and landslides, and deforestation fires in the Amazon.

population.value: About 14 million in 1890; about 203 million in the 2022 census.

urbanisation.value: Rapid move to cities after 1950; São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro are among the largest cities in the Americas.

disease.value: Yellow fever and smallpox campaigns (Oswaldo Cruz, 1904); Zika (2015); very high COVID-19 deaths.

migration.value: Large European immigration (Italians, Portuguese, Germans) and Japanese immigration (from 1908); internal migration from the north-east to the south-east.

economicBase.value: Coffee and rubber at first; later industry, soybeans, beef, iron ore and oil.

tradeRoutes.value: Atlantic shipping; today large exports to China, the US and Europe; a member of Mercosur (1991).

wealth.value: One of the ten largest economies, but with very uneven wealth.

moneyAndTax.value: Several currencies until the real (1994) ended very high inflation.

inequality.value: One of the most unequal countries in the world; slavery was abolished only in 1888, and Black Brazilians remain poorer on average.

governmentType.value: A federal presidential republic; military dictatorship 1964–1985; current constitution from 1988.

keyRulers.value: Getúlio Vargas (1930–1945, 1951–1954). Juscelino Kubitschek. Fernando Henrique Cardoso. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Dilma Rousseff. Jair Bolsonaro.

succession.value: Direct presidential elections since 1989, with electronic voting.

institutions.value: The National Congress, the Supreme Federal Court, 26 states and the Federal District.

stability.value: Coups in 1930 and 1964; the impeachment of presidents in 1992 and 2016; the 2023 attack on government buildings in Brasília.

eliteConflict.value: Power struggles between coffee-growing elites, the army and urban politicians in the early republic.

armyAndTech.value: The largest army in Latin America; a growing arms industry (Embraer aircraft).

majorWars.value: The War of Canudos (1896–97); sent troops to Italy in the Second World War (1944–45).

territoryChange.value: Acquired Acre from Bolivia (1903); borders mostly settled by diplomacy (Rio Branco).

alliancesRivals.value: Joined the Allies in both World Wars; a member of BRICS; a regional leader in South America.

inventions.value: Ethanol fuel from sugar cane (Proálcool programme, 1975); deep-water oil drilling; Embraer passenger jets.

scienceEducation.value: Public universities; the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation in medicine; Embrapa farming research.

openness.value: Protected industry for decades (to the 1990s), then opened to trade.

communicationTransport.value: Highways and air travel; Brasília built around roads; São Paulo Metro (1974).

religion.value: The largest Catholic population in the world; fast-growing Evangelical churches; Afro-Brazilian religions such as Candomblé.

languageWriting.value: Portuguese (the only Portuguese-speaking country in the Americas); many Indigenous languages.

artsArchitecture.value: Modernist architecture (Niemeyer), bossa nova, samba, telenovelas and football culture.

socialStructure.value: Large gaps between rich and poor and between white and Black or mixed-race Brazilians; favelas in big cities.

sharedIdentity.value: A mixed national identity drawing on African, Portuguese, Indigenous and immigrant roots, and football.

dailyLife.value: Apartments in cities and favelas on hillsides; rice, beans, feijoada; football in daily life.

neighbours.value: Borders ten countries: every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.

ideasReligions.value: Positivism shaped the early republic (the flag’s motto “Ordem e Progresso”).

colonisation.value: A former Portuguese colony; it expanded into the Amazon, clashing with Indigenous peoples.

riseSignals.value: The end of slavery (1888) and the army’s discontent led to the overthrow of Emperor Pedro II in 1889.

peakPeriod.value: The “Brazilian miracle” of fast growth (1968–73) and the 2000s commodity boom.

declineSignals.value: Debt crises in the 1980s and recessions in 2015–16; political polarisation.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Brazil; Wikipedia: History of Brazil (1889–present); IBGE census figures.
